platforms.title: Is Your Fatigue Iron Deficiency, or B12?
platforms.meta_description: Exhausted no matter how much you sleep? How the ASH tells iron-deficiency anemia apart from vitamin B12 deficiency, by tingling and nail changes.
platforms.body_html:
Exhausted no matter how much sleep you get, and reaching for an iron supplement without knowing for sure? The American Society of Hematology (ASH) explains that iron-deficiency anemia and vitamin B12 deficiency produce fatigue through completely different pathways. Taking random supplements without confirming the cause can leave the nutrient that's actually low still unaddressed.

Why the same fatigue has different causes

Iron-deficiency anemia is fatigue that comes from too little iron in the body, which lowers hemoglobin and leaves tissues without enough oxygen delivered to them. It's common in women with heavy periods, during pregnancy, and with gastrointestinal blood loss. Nails often thin out or curve into a spoon shape, and an unusual craving for non-food items like ice, known as pica, can show up alongside it.

Vitamin B12 deficiency comes from an entirely different pathway. It's marked by B12 being essential for nerve function and red blood cell production, so a shortage brings fatigue together with neurological symptoms like tingling or numbness in the hands and feet, poor balance, and foggy memory. It's common in people who've been vegetarian or vegan for a long time, older adults with reduced stomach acid, and anyone who's had stomach surgery.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether there's tingling or numbness in the hands and feet. The ASH notes this is a clear sign that shows up almost exclusively with B12 deficiency. Iron-deficiency anemia rarely brings any neurological symptoms along.

Second, whether the nails have thinned or curved, or there's an odd craving for something like ice. These signs lean toward iron-deficiency anemia and rarely show up with B12 deficiency.

What matters most is not taking random supplements without confirming which one is actually low. Taking extra iron when it isn't needed can build up in the body and cause harm, and while B12 is relatively safe, taking it without knowing the real cause can mean missing the testing and treatment that's actually needed. Both deficiencies are confirmed accurately with a blood test, so if symptoms continue, checking both iron levels and B12 levels together at a doctor's office is the safe move.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to note whether there's tingling in the hands or feet, any nail changes, usual eating habits including whether meat is eaten, and whether there's heavy menstrual bleeding or gastrointestinal blood loss. Left untreated long enough, B12 deficiency can leave permanent nerve damage, so tingling or memory changes are worth getting tested for without putting it off.

It's also worth noting that the two deficiencies can overlap, since a diet very low in meat can leave both iron and B12 running short at the same time, and some people end up with both showing up together on a blood panel. That's another reason to test for both rather than assuming it's only one or the other based on symptoms alone.

Along with the fatigue, do you also notice tingling in your hands or feet and foggy memory, or changes in your nails and an odd craving for ice?
